title: The Man Who Studied Stupidity
book: Poor Charlie's Almanack: The Essential Wit and Wisdom of Charles T. Munger
author: Charles T. Munger, edited by Peter D. Kaufman
wiifm: The week now turns from building wealth to keeping it. Charlie Munger lost a marriage, a son and an eye, and spent the rest of a very long life studying why clever people make ruinous decisions. His answers, from incentives to inversion to his checklist of human misjudgements, are some of the most practical tools for anyone running a business, setting commission schemes or weighing up a big move. You will follow him from a dentist's house in Omaha to a partnership with Warren Buffett, and you will leave with a short list of ways to be consistently not stupid.

b: Charles Thomas Munger was born in Omaha, Nebraska, on the first of January 1924. His father, Alfred, was a lawyer and his grandfather a federal judge, and the family lived a comfortable, orderly Midwestern life a short walk from a family called Buffett.

As a teenager Charlie worked on Saturdays at Buffett and Son, the grocery shop run by Warren Buffett's grandfather. The work was long and dull, the pay was poor, and old Ernest Buffett made his boys pay a couple of cents towards the new Social Security scheme while lecturing them on its evils. Warren, six years younger, worked there too, at a different time. The two did not meet properly for another two decades.

Munger was clever and restless and read biographies voraciously, especially of Benjamin Franklin, whose Poor Richard's Almanack gave his own book its title. He went to the University of Michigan to study mathematics, but in 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, he joined the Army Air Corps. He was trained as a meteorologist and posted to Nome, in Alaska.

After the war he got into Harvard Law School without an undergraduate degree, after a family friend intervened, and graduated in 1948. He moved to Los Angeles and became a lawyer. On paper, it was a smooth, successful start.
ch.cap: Teenage Charlie hauls crates at Buffett and Son

b: Then it fell apart. In 1953, when Munger was twenty-nine, his first marriage ended in divorce. He lost the family house and moved into a shabby room at the University Club. He drove a battered old car, and when a friend asked why, he said he was giving what he had to his children.

Shortly afterwards his son Teddy, aged about eight, was diagnosed with leukaemia. In the early 1950s there was no treatment. Munger would visit the hospital, hold his son, and then walk the streets of Pasadena weeping. Teddy died in 1955. Munger was thirty-one, divorced, short of money by the standards of his profession, and had buried a child.

He remarried in 1956, to Nancy Barry Borthwick, and together they raised a large blended family of eight children. But the losses were not finished. In 1980 a cataract operation went wrong, and complications left him in such pain that his left eye was removed. Fearing he might lose the other, he began learning Braille. He did not lose it, and wore thick glasses for the rest of his life.

This matters for how you read him. Poor Charlie's Almanack, a big collection of his speeches and sayings edited by Peter Kaufman and first published in 2005, is easy to treat as a rich man's list of clever one-liners. It is better understood as the lifelong effort of someone who had been genuinely broken to work out why capable people wreck things, and what discipline prevents it.
ch.cap: After the hospital, Munger walks Pasadena's streets weeping

b: In 1959 Munger went back to Omaha to settle his father's estate, and two friends arranged a dinner with Warren Buffett, who by then was running small investment partnerships. The two men talked so intensely that at one point Munger was reportedly laughing at his own jokes so hard he fell to the floor. They became friends, and Buffett kept telling him that law was a poor way for someone like him to get rich.

Munger agreed. In 1962 he co-founded a law firm, which became Munger, Tolles and Olson, and the same year set up an investment partnership, Wheeler, Munger and Company, trading from an office on the Pacific Coast Stock Exchange. Over fourteen years it compounded at almost twenty per cent a year, against a few per cent for the stock market. It also lost heavily in the crash of 1973 and 1974, around a third of its value in each year. Anyone tempted by his advice to hold only a few investments should remember that this is the price: losses of that size, arriving without warning.
Through the 1970s Munger and Buffett worked more and more closely, and in 1978 Munger became vice chairman of Buffett's company, Berkshire Hathaway. He held the post for forty-five years.
His great contribution was to change how Buffett invested, and to do that he first had to change how Buffett thought.
ch.cap: Munger laughs at his own jokes, dining with Buffett

ch.h: The candy shop that changed everything
b: Buffett had been trained by the investor Benjamin Graham to buy what he called cigar butts: mediocre businesses at prices so low that there was one free puff left in them. It worked, but it did not grow, because such bargains are small and rare and must be constantly replaced.

Munger argued that this was the wrong game. Pay a fair price for an excellent business, he said, and then leave it alone, because an excellent business keeps growing in value and a merely cheap one does not. His summary became famous: a great business at a fair price is better than a fair business at a great price.

The test came in 1972, with See's Candies, a Californian chocolate maker. The owners wanted thirty million dollars. Sales were around thirty million a year, pre-tax profits under five million, and the business had only about eight million dollars in hard assets. Buffett, by his own account, nearly walked away rather than pay more than three times the book value. The deal was done at twenty-five million. Munger pushed him to do it.

What See's had was not assets but pricing power. Its chocolates were bought as gifts, and people giving a box to someone they love worry more about looking cheap than about the price. So See's could raise prices most years without losing customers, and it needed almost no new money to grow. Over the following decades it produced around two billion dollars in pre-tax profits for Berkshire. Buffett has said that without See's they would never have bought Coca-Cola.

Munger added a behavioural rule he put crudely: the big money is not in the buying or the selling, but in the waiting. Patience is not laziness. It is a defence against all the forces that push people to do something.
ch.cap: A gift box at See's: buyers forgive a higher price

b: Munger's best-known idea is about how a mind is built. To a man with only a hammer, he liked to say, every problem looks like a nail. Professional training produces people with hammers. Economists explain everything with incentives, lawyers with rules, doctors with disease, marketers with branding, and each is right often enough to keep the habit going.

His remedy was to collect the really big ideas from all the major subjects, the few that carry most of the weight in each, and hold them together in what he called a latticework of mental models. Not hundreds. Perhaps eighty or ninety in all, of which a couple of dozen do most of the work. Then hang your experience on them.

The subjects he insisted on were not the obvious ones for an investor. Simple mathematics, especially compound interest and basic probability. Accounting, understood as a language with known limits. Engineering, for its ideas of backup systems and breaking points. Biology and evolution. And above all psychology, which he thought businessmen most lacked and most needed.

His other favourite tool came from the German mathematician Carl Jacobi, who told students to invert, always invert. Many hard problems are easier solved backwards. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you would guarantee failure, and then avoid that. Munger's own version was blunter: all he wanted to know was where he was going to die, so he would never go there.

In 1986, giving a speech at a school graduation, he refused to say how to be happy and instead gave a prescription for misery: be unreliable, learn only from your own experience, and when you suffer a setback, go down and stay down. Turned inside out, that is his whole advice on character.
ch.cap: One man has a hammer; Munger has a latticework

b: Of all his obsessions, the strongest was incentives. People always underestimate their power, he said, even after being told not to.

His favourite example came from Federal Express. Every package in its network passed through a central hub overnight, and if the planes were not loaded on time the whole system failed. For a long time the night shift could not finish on schedule. Management tried pep talks, supervision and moral pressure. Nothing worked. Then someone stopped paying the shift by the hour and paid them for the whole shift, letting them go home as soon as the planes were loaded. The problem vanished. Paying for hours buys hours. Paying for loaded planes buys loaded planes.

His second example was Xerox, where a new and better copier sold poorly while an older, worse machine sold well. The reason was the commission structure, which paid salesmen more for pushing the old one. Munger summed it up in an old saying: whose bread I eat, his song I sing. The salesmen were not wicked. They were responding sensibly to what they were actually paid for, which was not what the company said it wanted.

This leads to his idea of incentive-caused bias. People's judgement bends, sincerely and often unconsciously, towards whatever pays them. He was always wary of advice from any professional whose recommended course happened to be the one that paid them most, however much he liked them.

For anyone running a business where advice is given and a product sold, this is the question to ask of every pay scheme: is there any way the recommendation that is worse for the customer is better paid for the person making it? If so, it is not a training problem. It is a design problem.
ch.cap: Paid by the shift, the FedEx night crew races

b: The centrepiece of the Almanack is a talk Munger gave in several versions, most famously at Harvard in 1995, later written up as The Psychology of Human Misjudgment. It lists twenty-five standard ways that people go wrong. It is not academic psychology, and he was cheerfully rude about academic psychologists. It is a practitioner's field guide, drawing heavily on the work of Robert Cialdini on persuasion.

Some of the tendencies matter especially in business. Inconsistency avoidance: once we have announced a view, we resist changing it, especially in public. Doubt avoidance: we rush to decide, and the pressure is greatest just when things are most confusing, which is why salespeople create urgency. Social proof: when unsure, we copy others, sensible when fleeing a fire, disastrous in a market. Contrast: we judge against what we have just seen, so a high price shown first makes the next one feel reasonable.

Deprival superreaction is the pain of loss, which hurts far more than the pleasure of an equal gain, and it makes firms cling to a dying product because ending it feels like losing. There is excessive self-regard, overvaluing whatever is ours: our judgement, our hires, our plans. There is availability, where the vivid recent example beats the true average. And there is what he called twaddle, the confident noise from people with nothing to say, which crowds out real thinking.

The last tendency he called lollapalooza: extreme outcomes when several tendencies push in the same direction at once. They do not add, they multiply. His example was the Tupperware party, where hospitality, a friend as host, everyone else buying and a public commitment all act on you in one hour. Any one is resistible. Together they are close to irresistible. So when you review a mistake, do not look for the cause. Ask which three forces were all pushing the same way.
ch.cap: At a Tupperware party, every pressure pushes one way

b: The best piece in the book is a talk from 1996 in which Munger sets himself a puzzle. It is 1884 in Atlanta. A rich man called Glotz will put up two million dollars to start a soft drink business called Coca-Cola, but only if you can explain how it will be worth two trillion dollars by 2034. You have fifteen minutes.

He starts with law: the name must become a strongly protected trademark, or you have only invented a generic drink. Then arithmetic: by 2034 there will be around eight billion people, each needing about sixty-four ounces of water a day. If the drink captures a share of that, and the company keeps a profit of four cents on each eight-ounce serving, you reach roughly a hundred and seventeen billion dollars a year of earnings, enough to justify the valuation. The target is worked backwards from the answer.

Then psychology, used as engineering. Sugar and caffeine act as rewards. Every kind of association, from images to the name itself, builds a habit. Serve it cold, because the pleasure is greatest when people are hot. And the famous detail: the drink must have no aftertaste, because taste is how the body signals that you have had enough. Remove the aftertaste and people can drink far more, far more often. Finally, social proof: spend heavily on being everywhere, because being everywhere is itself part of the product.
Read once, it shows what a latticework actually does. Law, maths, physiology, conditioning and social psychology all do real work on one business question, and none would have answered it alone.
ch.cap: Glotz offers two million for a soft drink, Atlanta 1884

b: Munger stayed at Berkshire into extreme old age, famous at its annual meetings for sitting beside Buffett, eating peanut brittle, and answering long questions with a short phrase: I have nothing to add. He gave away much of his fortune, including large sums for university housing that he designed himself, often with very few windows, which caused some controversy.
He died in a California hospital on the twenty-eighth of November 2023, aged ninety-nine, thirty-four days before his hundredth birthday.

Three honest warnings come with his book. First, its psychology is drawn from observation and from work like Cialdini's, not from measured experiments, and since about 2011 a replication crisis has shown that many famous findings in social psychology were weaker than claimed. His list is a checklist for noticing, not proven science with known effect sizes. Second, with eighty mental models to hand, a clever person can explain any outcome after the event and feel rigorous doing it. The only real discipline is to write down what you expect before you find out. Third, his advice to concentrate on a few big bets came with those heavy losses in 1973 and 1974. Be honest about whether your nerves, and your obligations, could take that.

What remains is a practical philosophy for anyone protecting what they have built. It is remarkable, he said, how much long-term advantage people like him and Buffett had gained by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent. Because returns compound, avoiding the one catastrophic mistake is worth more than adding one clever move.
Tomorrow you meet a man who made exactly that catastrophic mistake, in public, and built an entire system to stop it happening again.
ch.cap: Munger beside Buffett on stage: I have nothing to add

take: Write next to each commission, bonus or target the behaviour it literally rewards. Then ask how the laziest, most self-interested person would maximise it without breaking a rule.
Ask whether any recommendation that is worse for the customer is better paid for the person making it. If so, fix the pay design rather than the training.
Before a big decision, write the story of how it failed eighteen months from now. Insure against the cheap risks that afternoon, and take seriously the one nobody wanted to mention.
See's Candies earned billions because of pricing power, not cheap assets. When choosing products, partners or acquisitions, favour quality you can keep over bargains you must keep replacing.
Do not solve every problem with the tool your job taught you. Borrow ideas from psychology, maths and engineering, and ask what each would say about the problem.
Big mistakes rarely have one cause. When reviewing one, ask which several forces were pushing the same way at once.
Mental models can explain anything afterwards. Record what you expect before you find out, then check, so you learn rather than rationalise.
Because gains compound, dodging the one catastrophic error beats adding a clever win. Size every risk so that being wrong is survivable.
recall: What changed at Federal Express, and why did it work?
The night shift stopped being paid by the hour and was paid for the shift, free to go home once the planes were loaded. Paying for hours bought hours; paying for loaded planes bought loaded planes.
What did Munger change about Buffett's investing, and what was the test case?

He moved Buffett from buying cheap mediocre businesses, cigar butts, to paying fair prices for excellent ones. The test was See's Candies in 1972, bought for twenty-five million dollars, which produced around two billion in pre-tax profit thanks to its pricing power.
What is inversion, and where did Munger get it?
Solving a problem backwards by asking how to guarantee failure and then avoiding it. He took it from the mathematician Carl Jacobi's advice to invert, always invert.

Extreme outcomes produced when several psychological tendencies push in the same direction at once, multiplying rather than adding. The Tupperware party, combining hospitality, liking, social proof and commitment, is his example.
Why must Glotz's drink have no aftertaste?
Because taste is the body's signal to stop. Without an aftertaste, people can drink far more, more often, which makes the market share arithmetic possible.

The chocolate shop that changed Buffett

In 1972 a Californian sweet maker called See's Candies came up for sale. The owners wanted thirty million dollars for a business with only about eight million in hard assets. Warren Buffett, trained to buy things cheap, nearly walked away. Munger pushed him to pay up, and the deal was done at twenty-five million. The secret was gifts: people buying chocolates for someone they love will not risk looking cheap, so See's could raise prices almost every year and needed hardly any new money to grow. Over the following decades it earned Berkshire around two billion dollars before tax. Buffett has said that without See's they would never have bought Coca-Cola.

In 1996 Munger set himself a puzzle. It is 1884 in Atlanta, and a rich man will fund a new soft drink called Coca-Cola, but only if you can explain in fifteen minutes how it will be worth two trillion dollars by 2034. Munger worked it through: protect the trademark, do the arithmetic on billions of thirsty people, serve it cold, use sugar and caffeine as rewards, and be everywhere so that ubiquity becomes part of the product. His cleverest detail was to make sure the drink leaves no aftertaste, because aftertaste is how the body says enough. Remove it, and people drink far more.
biz: Run the Xerox test on every pay plan

Xerox salesmen pushed the worse copier because it paid more. Ask the same of your brokers and debt advisers this week: is any recommendation that is worse for the customer better paid for the person making it? Check whether pay rises with loan size, lender commission or, in debt advice, with one solution type over another. If it does, redesign rather than retrain. Reward file quality, suitable outcomes, low complaints and good customer feedback. Measure the mix of lenders and solutions per adviser monthly, and investigate anyone whose mix drifts towards the best paid option.

Munger asked how to guarantee failure, then avoided it. Write down how you would make sure a frightened debt client never calls back or ends up complaining: a missed callback, jargon, a pushy WhatsApp late at night, rushing past signs of vulnerability, warnings buried in small print. Then check your current process against that list and fix the worst three. Guard against the lollapalooza too: urgency, social proof and commitment combined in an ad or script can overwhelm someone in distress. Track callback times, drop out points and vulnerability flags recorded.
connects: Munger's twenty-five tendencies, and especially his lollapalooza of social proof, commitment and reciprocity at the Tupperware party, draw directly on Cialdini's work on persuasion.
Munger's checklist of misjudgements is the practitioner's version of Kahneman's research into the systematic biases of fast, intuitive thinking.
Munger's habit of running a mental checklist of misjudgements before a decision shares Gawande's insight that simple checklists catch the errors that even experts make.
recap:
Charlie Munger was born in Omaha in nineteen twenty-four, a short walk from the Buffett family, and worked Saturdays in their grocery shop. He became a wartime weather forecaster in Alaska, got into Harvard Law School without a first degree, and settled in Los Angeles as a lawyer. Then, in his early thirties, his life fell apart. His marriage ended, he lost the house, and his son Teddy, aged about eight, died of leukaemia. Munger would hold the boy in hospital and then walk the streets of Pasadena weeping. Decades later a failed cataract operation cost him an eye.

Out of that grief came a lifelong study of why clever people make ruinous decisions. In nineteen fifty-nine he met Warren Buffett at a dinner in Omaha, and the two became partners for life.

His first big idea changed how Buffett invested. A great business at a fair price beats a fair business at a great price. See's Candies cost twenty-five million dollars and went on to earn around two billion, because people buying chocolates as a gift will happily pay a little more each year. And the big money, he said, is in the waiting.

The second idea is the latticework. To a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail, so collect the big ideas from many subjects, from compound interest to evolution to psychology, and let them work together.

The third is inversion. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you would be sure to fail, and avoid that. All he wanted to know, he joked, was where he was going to die, so he would never go there.

The fourth is incentives. At Federal Express the night shift kept missing its deadline until people were paid for the whole shift instead of by the hour. Then the planes left on time. Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.

The fifth is his list of twenty-five ways the mind goes wrong, and the warning that the worst disasters come when several of them push the same way at once. He called that a lollapalooza.

Treat that psychology as a checklist rather than settled science, because many findings have since proved weaker than claimed, and remember that his concentrated bets once lost about a third of their value in each of two bad years.

He died in twenty twenty-three, thirty-four days short of his hundredth birthday. Keep his most famous observation: it is remarkable how much long-term advantage he and Buffett gained by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent.
